title: 40,000 troops foundered on one island, half a continent sold for $15 million: the rise and fall of the second-largest colonial empire, and eight lessons for anyone selling wall stickers overseas
summary: The rise and fall of the second-largest colonial empire contains a few accounts that look uncannily like today's business: 40,000 troops lost in Haiti, Louisiana sold for $15 million, and rubber plantations where workers went out as men and came back as skeletons. From product selection and cutting losses to brand premium and a graceful exit, here are eight lessons for anyone taking goods global.
author: starteday Editorial
body: Having covered the Dutch East India Company, this time it's France's turn. At its peak its colonial empire covered 12.347 million square kilometres — nearly a tenth of the world's land surface — making it the second-largest colonial empire after Britain, with more than 100 million people under its rule. But the most interesting thing about this imperial story is not how big it got; it is a handful of accounts that look strikingly like business ledgers today.

Start with the beginnings. France was a late entrant: Port Royal was founded in Nova Scotia in 1605, and Champlain built Quebec City in 1608 — that was New France. Rather than scramble with Spain and Portugal for gold and silver mines, it stuck patiently to the fur trade. Beaver-felt hats were all the rage among European aristocrats, North American beavers carried thick coats, and the cargoes kept flowing home.

That beginning points to a plain truth: big businesses rarely start by chasing the next big thing. They start by catching a real need. Cross-border trade is no different. Wall stickers aren't glamorous, but plenty of people rent homes abroad, don't want to damage the walls, have limited budgets and still want to change the look of a room. That need is real, constant and indifferent to seasons. Find your 'beaver-felt hat' first; talk about everything else afterwards.

Then the bitterest lesson. At the end of the 18th century, France's most valuable overseas possession was not the North American wilderness but Saint-Domingue in the Caribbean — today's Haiti. Just over 50,000 square kilometres, it produced two-thirds of France's overseas trade, with sugar making up 40 per cent of world output and coffee 60 per cent. After the uprising broke out in 1789, Napoleon sent his brother-in-law Leclerc across the sea at the head of an army of 40,000 to crush it, vowing to take the island back.

What followed was guerrilla warfare plus yellow fever. More than 30,000 men were lost in two years; Leclerc himself died of disease on the island; in 1803 the remnants surrendered and Haiti won independence. Napoleon's most valuable overseas asset simply burned away. The lesson for anyone going global: the most profitable business is often the most dangerous one. When it starts to fail, people instinctively double down to rescue it and end up staking the whole fortune. Don't keep fighting for sunk costs.

With the American dream in ruins, Napoleon reacted with startling speed. On 11 April 1803 the American envoy had come only to discuss buying the port of New Orleans. French foreign minister Talleyrand opened with a question: 'What would you pay for all of it?' Three weeks later the deal was signed: 2.14 million square kilometres of Louisiana for $15 million. Napoleon explained it bluntly afterwards — the money met an urgent need on the European battlefield and, as a bonus, 'gave Britain a formidable rival'.

An asset turning toxic in your hands should be cashed out while someone is still willing to take it, with the proceeds redirected to a battlefield you can actually win. In business today that means killing loss-making lines, recovering cash and concentrating resources on the main channel. If a pattern's test numbers look bad, pull it however reluctant you feel. One fewer unsold roll in the warehouse is one more measure of freedom on the balance sheet.

France governed its colonies with a different pitch from everyone else's. It spoke of a 'civilising mission' and of assimilation — teaching French, teaching people that 'our ancestors were the Gauls'. Its colonial schools taught few pupils very much, yet more than a century on, French remains the official language of 29 countries, and Parisian fashion, champagne and cosmetics still collect a premium on the word 'French'.

This may be the lesson in French colonial history most worth pondering for anyone going global: the product is physical, the premium is cultural. Take the same wall sticker, give it an original pattern with genuine aesthetic sense, a credible brand story and a presentable website, and in the customer's eyes it stops being a cheap sheet of plastic and becomes 'the solution for my walls'. Branding isn't mysterious. It is simply trust, kept consistently over time.

In territorial terms, the French army seized Algiers in 1830, opening the second colonial empire. Tunisia, Morocco, the whole sweep of West Africa into Central Africa, Madagascar and Indochina followed. After the First World War came the mandates over Syria and Lebanon, and between 1919 and 1939 the empire peaked at 12.347 million square kilometres and 110 million people. In 1931 Paris staged a colonial exhibition, and eight million French people queued to see it.

The other side of the ledger is cold. Colonies were deliberately kept as suppliers of a single raw material, industry was forbidden, administrative costs regularly outran tax revenue, and the cost of holding it all kept mounting. Within a few years of that 1931 exhibition, the empire's hole in the accounts could no longer be concealed. It is the common failing of any big spread: scale goes up while marginal profit comes down. Everyone in cross-border trade knows it — by the tenth platform and the thirtieth SKU is exactly when losses come easiest. Going deep in one market is worth more than covering ten.

Indochina was the empire's most painful nerve. Governor Doumer funded a third of local expenditure from monopoly taxes on opium, alcohol and salt. Rice exports ranked third in the world, yet the farmers who grew the rice could not eat their fill. Nothing exposes the imbalance better than the rubber plantations. Companies such as Michelin enclosed land in the red-earth region of southern Vietnam, expanding from 200 hectares in 1908 to 126,000 hectares by 1940. More than 100,000 northern labourers were recruited to the south, put to work twelve hours a day, and suffered first-year death rates of 30 to 40 per cent.

A Vietnamese folk song puts it this way: 'They go as men; they come back as skeletons.' A business that piles all its costs onto other people and pumps every profit back to Paris may look good on the quarterly sheet, but the reckoning arrives in the end — strikes, resistance, independence, each in turn. The modern equivalents are plain enough: squeeze suppliers until they cannot survive, make after-sales service a token gesture, treat bad reviews as noise. Each is a thorn you will have to pull out later. Better to pay a little more for the glue and make sure whoever stuck up the first sheet wants a second.

The empire ended with the shot fired at Dien Bien Phu on 7 May 1954. French forces in Indochina were encircled and destroyed, more than 10,000 surrendered, and the Geneva Accords sent France packing from the peninsula. That same year the Algerian war of independence broke out; it ran for eight years, costing millions of casualties without producing a single victory, and closed with the Évian Accords in 1962. In 1960 alone, fourteen colonies south of the Sahara became independent together — the year remembered as the 'Year of Africa'.

What is striking is that de Gaulle's France, knowing full well it could not hold on, chose to negotiate, withdraw and trade. Put into business language, the lesson is to tell the difference between 'still winnable' and 'merely refusing to admit defeat'. When platform rules change, a category declines across the board and every effort to save the stock only buries you deeper, scaling back in time and leaving with dignity — keeping your powder dry for the next battlefield — is worth far more than staying put and talking about sentiment.

The empire scattered, but the 'invisible assets' France left behind are what repay study. It still holds 13 overseas territories and an exclusive economic zone of about 11.6 million square kilometres, the second-largest in the world; the monetary systems of 14 African countries remain tied to the franc to this day; French, legal systems and educational networks still run through the former colonies. The hard occupation is gone, yet the web woven from rules, currency, language and brand keeps working. Historians call it the 'invisible empire'.

The last lesson for today's exporters is hidden here: only the assets you can carry away are truly yours. A platform shop can be closed at a stroke; a best-seller can become obsolete in a season. What follows you is brand recognition, customer trust and channel relationships. Selling wall stickers abroad, we have no wish to build an empire — only to make the pattern, adhesive and after-sales service of every sheet dependable, so that people renting on a tight budget can turn four blank walls into something they like with their own hands, so that those who have put one up come back for another and recommend it to others. Not an empire: a small brand built to last.
